name: Where the Rain Keeps Its Umbrellas
description: A hare without an umbrella follows the drizzle to a very old tree, and finds that the best umbrellas are the ones we share.

chapters.title: No Umbrella
chapters.illustrationAlt: A small hare in a yellow scarf walks along a muddy path in a soft drizzle, past puddles and wet green hills.
text: It was a gray, soft, drizzly Tuesday, and Wick the hare was out of umbrellas. He had owned three. The first had blown away in March, the second had been borrowed by a goose, and the third had a hole in it the exact shape of a hare.

Wick did not mind the drizzle, really. It was the kind of rain that does not fall so much as float. But he did have an errand. He was carrying a jar of blackberry jam to his Aunt Tansy on the other side of the valley, and he had a feeling that jam, like toast, was best kept dry.

So he turned up his collar, wrapped his yellow scarf twice around his neck, and set off down the muddy road, humming. The puddles were full of small gray skies. A snail went by on the verge with a leaf over his shell, looking smug.

"Excuse me," called Wick. "Where did you find your umbrella?" The snail considered the question for a long time. "It found me," he said at last. "They say the rain keeps a whole stock of them in the old hollow oak. Follow the drip."

chapters.title: Follow the Drip
chapters.illustrationAlt: A big old oak with a hollow door and dozens of colorful umbrellas hanging from its branches like leaves.
text: Wick followed the drip. It was easier than it sounds. Every few steps a bead of water fell from a leaf and landed on a stone with a tiny plink, and each plink seemed to point a little further along the path.

The road turned into a lane, and the lane into a trail, and the trail wound through a damp green wood where the moss was thick enough to sit on. Then, at the edge of a clearing, Wick stopped. In front of him stood the oldest oak he had ever seen.

Its trunk was as wide as a cottage. Its roots rose out of the ground like sleepy elbows. And hanging from every branch, as if they were leaves, were umbrellas. Red ones and green ones, polka-dotted and striped, tiny ones for beetles and enormous ones for bears. They swayed in the drizzle, and the raindrops landed on them with a sound like very quiet applause.

"Hello?" called Wick. A small wooden sign on the trunk said, in curly writing, TAKE ONE, LEAVE ONE, SHARE ONE. Wick read it twice. It was a very good rule, and not at all difficult. He looked up, and among all the umbrellas, one yellow one with a little white cloud painted on it turned slightly toward him, as if it had been waiting.

chapters.title: Take One, Leave One, Share One
text: Wick took the yellow umbrella down. It opened with a soft, pleased pop, and the drizzle stopped tapping on his ears. It was the most comfortable thing he had ever held. It seemed to be exactly the right size for a hare with a jar of jam.

Then he remembered the sign. Take one, leave one. He had nothing to leave. He looked in his pockets and found a button, a stub of pencil and a rather nice smooth stone. He hung the stone on a low branch, and the oak seemed to accept it graciously. A small umbrella nearby tilted, as if to say that was fine.

"That leaves share one," murmured Wick. And just then, he heard a sniffle. At the edge of the clearing, a young duckling stood in the drizzle, soaked right through, her feathers pressed flat. "I lost my mother in the fog," she said. "And now I am very wet and a little bit lost."

Wick did not need to think about it. He crouched down, held the yellow umbrella over her, and said, "I am going to Aunt Tansy's. She has a stove and a spare bed, and she is very good at finding mothers." The duckling blinked up at him and, after a moment, tucked herself under his arm.

They set off together, a hare and a duckling under a single yellow umbrella. The jam jar knocked gently against Wick's hip. The drizzle fell softly. And for the first time that day, Wick noticed that it was not gray at all. It was silver.

chapters.title: The Shortcut
text: The road to Aunt Tansy's had two ways to go. The long way wound around the valley, past the mill and the stone bridge. The short way cut straight through the Whispering Reeds, where the path was narrow and the mud was thick.

"Shortcut," said Wick, and the duckling nodded. But when they reached the edge of the reeds, they found a small, worried hedgehog sitting on a stump, looking at the water. "The path is under a puddle," he said. "It is a very deep puddle. I was thinking of going home."

Wick looked at the puddle. It was wide and brown, and it was getting wider as the drizzle fell. He looked at his boots, which were old, and at the jam jar, which was precious. Then he looked at the hedgehog, who had a sack of chestnuts, and had clearly been standing there for a long time.

"We could go the long way," said Wick. "Together." The hedgehog brightened. "I do like the long way," he said. "It has a bridge." It was not exactly true, since the short way was not very much shorter, and the long way, as it turned out, was beautiful. There were blackberry bushes and a field of sleepy sheep, and a mill with a wheel that turned in the rain.
They arrived at Aunt Tansy's gate a little later than they would have, and a good deal happier, and it was only on the doorstep that Wick realized he had never once felt hurried.

chapters.title: The Biggest Umbrella
chapters.illustrationAlt: A crowd of small animals huddle happily together under one huge umbrella, with rain falling softly around them.
text: On the road to Aunt Tansy's, the hedgehog with the chestnuts walked close beside Wick, humming the same three notes over and over, and soon they met more travelers. "Room for one more?" said Wick, to nobody in particular, and it turned out there was.

First came two squirrels who had been sheltering under a mushroom and were glad to move. Then a goose, who was embarrassed about the third umbrella. And a very old, very quiet tortoise who said nothing but looked so pleased to be asked that Wick felt something warm go all the way down to his toes.

The yellow umbrella was not a big one. But it did something that umbrellas from the old oak do. It grew. It stretched a little with each new passenger, like a held breath, until it was wide enough to cover every one of them, and still had a little room left for the rain to patter on.

They walked together slowly, because that is the speed at which an umbrella full of friends goes. The squirrels told a story about an acorn that grew into a staircase. The goose apologized to Wick about the third umbrella, and Wick said it was quite all right, as it had led him to the oak.

When they reached Aunt Tansy's little house, there was smoke curling from the chimney and a lamp glowing in the window. And on the doorstep, with a mug of cocoa and a very relieved face, was a mother duck. "There you are," she said to the duckling, and the whole umbrella went quiet and warm, like the inside of a hug.

chapters.title: Aunt Tansy's Kitchen
text: Aunt Tansy's kitchen was the warmest room in the valley. It had a black stove with a kettle that never quite stopped murmuring, a long scrubbed table, and so many jars of jam on the shelves that the light from the window came through them in red and purple and gold.

She did not seem at all surprised to see a hare, a duckling, a hedgehog, two squirrels, a goose and a tortoise on her doorstep. "Come in, come in," she said. "Boots by the door. There is always room for one more at my table, and today it appears there is room for eight."

Wick handed over the jar of blackberry jam, a little proudly, and Aunt Tansy held it up to the light, so that the whole kitchen glowed purple. "My favorite," she said, "and not a drop spilled." The umbrella, hung on a hook by the stove, was dripping gently into a pot, and had shrunk back to its original size with the air of an umbrella who had done a good day's work.

They ate jam on toast, and bowls of soup, and a rather large plum cake that appeared from somewhere. The duckling fell asleep at the table with a crumb on her beak. The goose finally got to apologize properly, and Aunt Tansy said it was the nicest apology she had had all year.

chapters.title: Leave One
text: The next morning the drizzle had gone, and the valley was washed and shining. Wick said goodbye to everyone, and then he did something he had been thinking about since the oak. He took the yellow umbrella down from its hook.

He walked back through the damp green wood with it folded under his arm. At the old hollow oak he stopped and looked up at all the umbrellas hanging in the branches, still and dry. "I was told to take one, leave one and share one," he said, to the tree. "I think I have done two out of three properly. I left a stone. It does not seem enough."

He found, in his pocket, a nicely smooth button, and a stub of pencil. He thought for a while. Then he borrowed a bit of bark from the ground and, with the pencil, drew on it a tiny picture of a yellow umbrella and a duckling and a hare. He hung it carefully on a low branch.

The oak rustled. High up, something small and green turned toward him, and slowly, one by one, the umbrellas swayed, the red ones and the green ones and the polka-dotted, as if the whole tree were nodding. Wick smiled, hung the yellow umbrella back in its place, and walked home through the sunshine with his hands in his pockets, humming.
